extracted.intended_audience: journalists, newsroom editors, media scholars, and policymakers concerned with news quality and democratic effects
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for news organizations and journalists about news tone (soft vs hard), investigative standards, the watchdog role, audience preferences, and how coverage affects public trust and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: Negative vs Positive Coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative coverage of politics has risen dramatically (e.g., negative coverage of presidential candidates now exceeds positive coverage; by 1990, negative coverage of Congress and its members was over 80%). The press shows a pronounced tendency to report what is wrong with politics and politicians rather than what is right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive negativity erodes political trust and interest. Editors should avoid a constant presumption that politicians are incompetent or venal and balance critical reporting with fair assessment of accomplishments and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in Government (impact metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trust in government has dropped sharply over the past four decades (Figure 13). Trust sometimes rises (e.g., in response to a stronger economy) but has not returned to earlier levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declining trust is an important outcome to monitor when assessing news tone and public-affairs coverage; negative news contributes to weakened attachments to politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived Honesty of Politicians (impact metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion of Americans who think most government officials are honest has dropped substantially and is roughly half what it was in 1968 (Figure 14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes in this perception signal consequences of media framing and scandal coverage; reporters should consider how coverage affects long-term trust in institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest in Public Affairs (audience metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest in public affairs has declined (e.g., those saying they are interested 'most of the time' fell from ~35% to 25%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower public interest reduces news consumption; news organizations should weigh how story selection and tone influence long-term civic engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Perception Predicts Attention
rubrics_metrics.description: The best predictor of whether people report paying 'less' rather than 'more' attention to news is the perception that today's news is 'negative' rather than 'positive' (among those paying less attention, 93% perceive news as largely negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perceived negativity directly reduces audience attention; monitoring perceived tone is critical for audience-retention strategies and civic implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft News vs Hard News Distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Soft news (incident-driven, entertainment-style) differs from hard news (major events and public affairs). Negative headlines attracted more interest than positive ones on average for soft news; for hard news the positive versions actually drew slightly more interest on average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers should recognize that tone interacts with story type: sensational negative tone may boost short-term interest in soft news but can be counterproductive for public-affairs/hard-news audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content over Tone (topic trumps valence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone was less important than content; for example, both positive and negative headlines about Middle East conflict drew more interest than either version of a headline about drug charges involving a pro football player.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should prioritize substantive, high-salience topics; manipulating tone alone is a weaker strategy for sustaining audience interest than selecting important content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of 'Bad News Sells' (subject-area caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: While negative headlines attracted more interest on average, the difference was not large and 'bad news' does not uniformly attract more interest across all subject areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relying on negativity as a universal formula for engagement is risky; audience responses vary by topic and over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative Journalism Standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Top-notch investigative journalism requires thorough scrutiny of officials' behavior and substantial time and effort to determine the validity of claims or to prove wrongdoing (e.g., Watergate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-quality investigation is resource- and time-intensive; newsrooms should allocate sufficient time and resources and resist 24-hour-cycle pressures that make sustained investigation nearly impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Sources vs Deep Investigation (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Much negative content is supplied through journalists' use of adversarial sources rather than deep investigation. When politicians make statements, reporters often turn to adversaries to attack it—a routine insertion of counter-claims that supports controversy rather than careful assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid defaulting to adversary-sourced conflict as a substitute for verification; favor independent assessment and evidence over dispute framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter as Participant: Balance of Reporter vs Newsmaker Voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters increasingly become direct participants in coverage (e.g., in 2000 reporters spoke six minutes for every minute candidates' words on broadcast coverage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive to keep newsmakers' voices central and avoid over-centering reporters' judgments; ensure adequate balance between reported statements and reporter commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norm of Partisan Neutrality But No Norm Limiting Negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic norms constrain partisan bias but do not constrain negativity; thus a press can be nonpartisan in slant yet highly negative in tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uphold impartiality while creating newsroom norms or editorial checks that guard against excessive, reflexive negativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchdog Role: Distinguish Real Abuse from Small Errors
rubrics_metrics.description: A watchdog press must have the judgment to distinguish real abuse of power from small errors of judgment and performance; failing to do so 'poisons the well' and can weaken public trust in both officials and the media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise proportionality and standards of evidence; avoid sensationalizing minor lapses and calibrate scrutiny to the gravity of alleged misconduct (Lewinsky coverage cited as an example of excess).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of More Credible Journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Credible journalism should not ignore official wrongdoing, should not turn the media agenda over to newsmakers, should give proper voice to the newsmakers, pay sufficient attention to what government is doing well, and assess politicians' failings by reasonable standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt practices that combine skepticism with fairness: investigate wrongdoing but also report accomplishments and provide context; these behaviors help restore trust and renew interest in news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Sensationalism and Intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-affairs reporting is widely perceived as too negative, too sensational, and too intrusive; lurid, hearsay-rooted coverage can backfire and cause the public to reject media outcries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit sensationalism, protect ordinary privacy unless public-interest justification is clear, and emphasize verification over lurid detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey Metrics for News Consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Operational measures used in the survey include: how much attention respondents normally pay to government/public-affairs; childhood household news exposure; frequency of reading newspaper/watching national or local TV news/listening to radio/following internet news; whether they watch most of a newscast; and whether they are regular users of a medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures provide standardized ways to classify 'regular' news consumers and to relate consumption patterns to preferences and political interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: News Preference Importance Criteria (audience values)
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked what is important in news (SN-19), respondents rated: 'Is lively and enjoyable'; 'Fits easily into your daily schedule'; 'Is timely and up to date'; 'Provides information that helps you to understand public affairs'; 'Provides information that helps you in your daily life'; 'Tells you about the good things and the bad things that happen to ordinary people'; 'Stirs your emotions and feelings'; 'Is substantial rather than sensational.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these dimensions to evaluate news formats and editorial mixes against audience priorities; note that different audience segments weight these criteria differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline Test Methodology (evaluating tone effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental method where two versions of each headline (positive and negative) were administered to respondents (half positive, half negative) to measure how tone affects interest in reading a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This controlled manipulation isolates the effect of tone from content and can inform decisions about headline framing for different story types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience Segmentation: 'Busy' People Prefer Hard News
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-described 'busy' people show a stronger preference for hard news and less tolerance for soft news; by a 3-1 ratio, busy people place a premium on public affairs information and prefer tightly packaged news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment audiences and tailor formats: busy audiences favor concise, substantive public-affairs reporting rather than soft, entertainment-style content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soft News Prevalence and Long-term Audience Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Shrinking audiences have led to more soft news and critical reporting; over time, soft and negative news distort public understanding and reduce interest in news and public affairs, harming both democracy and long-term audience sustainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance short-term audience-capture tactics (soft/negative stories) with long-term investment in balanced public-affairs reporting to sustain and rebuild a civic news habit.
